problem: The sentence "With two or more symbols, every code word has at least one bit, so L = 1 even when H is small" is false for three or more symbols. Only with exactly two symbols must both code words be 1 bit long, giving L = 1. With four symbols, for example, L can be 2 bits as in the worked example that follows, so a student reading this will expect L = 1 everywhere.
fix: With exactly two symbols, both code words must be 1 bit long, so L = 1 even when H is small (for p = 0.9 and 0.1, H ≈ 0.469 but L = 1). With more symbols the code words take different lengths and L can be larger than 1.

problem: Saying a symbol with p = 0.9 "needs about 0.152 bits, not 1 bit" overstates it for a single symbol. 0.152 bits is the self-information of that symbol; arithmetic coding reaches that average cost only over a long message, and any real encoder must also spend bits to end the message.
fix: In a long message with p = 0.9, arithmetic coding spends about −log₂ 0.9 = 0.152 bits per occurrence of that symbol on average, against a full 1 bit for Huffman. A single short message still costs whole bits plus a termination cost.

problem: "Any number inside the final interval identifies the message" leaves out how the decoder knows the message has ended. Without a length or an end-of-message symbol, the decoder keeps mapping the number and emits extra symbols.
fix: The encoder also sends the message length, or uses a special end-of-message symbol, so the decoder stops after the right number of symbols.

problem: The first sentence defines an entropy coder as one that gives short code words to likely symbols, then lumps run-length coding under "These coders". RLE does not shorten code words by probability; it replaces repeats by counts, and it can make a file bigger.
fix: Say that Huffman and arithmetic coding are entropy coders, while run-length coding is a simple repeat-collapsing coder that is often used before an entropy coder.
